# Easel

Oct 31, 2026 · @Guy-robert

## Product direction

A shared multimodal canvas where people and agents explore, create, and revise ideas together. Learning a technical topic, planning a project, building a mockup, and brainstorming are all uses of the same collaboration model, so the product is not limited to one subject or to tutoring.

The bet is that people prefer working with agents this way over chat. Individual features do not need to be novel. What matters is the quality of continuous collaboration: both participants work on the same objects, and text, voice, ink, and comments all change the same board state.

Two repeatable sessions are the test bed for every change: exploring a physics concept and developing a project mockup.

## Interaction model

The user and the AI work on one infinite canvas. Both act through the same set of primitives, and every action changes shared board state that the other side can see.

| Primitive | User | AI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ask | Types or speaks with nothing selected | Asks the user a question, by voice or as a note |
| Annotate | Circles, underlines, or highlights an element, then types or speaks about it | Highlights an element and attaches a note or arrow to it |
| Manipulate | Drags a slider, moves an object, changes a parameter | Sets parameters on graphs and simulations |
| Sketch | Draws a freehand diagram or curve | Turns a sketch into a precise shape |
| Predict | Places a guess before a result is shown | Requests a prediction, then reveals the result next to it |

The AI acts when the user addresses it by voice or text. It may also act after the user pauses: a change on the board starts a debounce of about 1.5 s, any new user interaction cancels the pending check, and changes the agent made itself never start one. When the check runs, staying quiet is a valid outcome.

## Board layout

One board per topic or project. When the user asks for something, the AI first places a map: a row of empty tldraw frames, one per part, each with a title and a one-line description of what it will hold. For Fourier transforms that might be intuition, the math, a worked example, and applications. For a mockup it might be goals, user flow, screens, and open decisions. The AI then fills the frames one at a time, so the user can start working in the first frame while later ones are still being generated. The user can cancel or retry generation per frame.

The area to the left of the map is the user's space for scratch work, drawings, and their own notes. Protected regions are enforced in code: agent commands that target them are rejected unless the user asked for that change. New AI content goes next to the frame it relates to, and the user's camera stays where it is while the agent adds content elsewhere.

The user can ask the AI to add a frame, split one into smaller parts, or go deeper on one part. Each of those runs the same skeleton-then-fill process on a smaller scope.

## Architecture

[embedded content: Components and how they connect\]

The Swift shell handles the hotkey and screen capture and hosts the web app. The canvas and the voice model both change the board through the agent backend's canvas tools. The backend calls a frontier model for topic maps and new visualizations, and runs Manim jobs in the background.

## Canvas and shapes

The canvas is the current tldraw SDK (5.6.0 on npm as of November 2) in a React app, starting from the tldraw agent starter kit at the matching version. Reuse the starter's context collection, validated actions, streaming, and cancellation, and extend its shape schemas so the agent can read and edit custom parameters. tldraw is free on localhost. Shipping it, including inside a desktop app, requires a tldraw license key.

Built-in tldraw shapes cover notes, text, arrows, frames, highlights, and freehand strokes. Interactive content uses custom shapes that host React components:

| Shape | Renders with | Parameters both sides can set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GraphShape` | Mafs or JSXGraph | Function, domain, marked points, sliders |
| `SimShape` | Three.js with a physics step in code | Simulation type and its parameters, such as launch angle and initial velocity |
| `EquationShape` | KaTeX | LaTeX source, highlighted terms |
| `DiagramShape` | D3 | Nodes, edges, layout |
| `VideoShape` | HTML video | Source file from a Manim render |

Each custom shape stores its parameters in tldraw shape props, so a change from either side is a normal board update and syncs to everything else that reads the board.

Shapes expose stable shape and part IDs, such as `g1.curve` or `eq3.term2`, so annotations, pointing, and agent commands can target parts of a shape.

### Visual direction

The board should feel like paper: warm paper tones, dark ink, an editorial serif for prose, a clean sans-serif for controls, generous spacing, and low surface contrast. Content looks typeset onto the canvas, and frames organize it quietly instead of enclosing everything in cards or sticky notes. Selection outlines and contextual controls appear when needed, and permanent interface chrome stays small. Body text starts around 17 to 18 px at reading zoom. Source Serif 4 is a candidate for the serif, to be compared against reference typography before it is chosen. Text wrapping, selection, equation alignment, and editing get refined before decorative motion. tldraw custom themes and rich text cover most of this.

## Agent and canvas tools

The agent backend is a local TypeScript process that shares shape schemas and the command model with the frontend. Every board change, from the UI or the agent, is a validated command, so there is one code path for every change.

- Each command records its origin: user, agent, or voice.
- Dragging and other direct manipulation apply locally and immediately. The command is recorded after the fact.
- Agent commands carry the board revision they were based on. A command whose target changed since then is rejected as stale.
- Commands into protected user regions are rejected.
- Cancel stops future agent work. Revert is a separate action, and reverting agent work never removes newer human work.

The agent's tools are commands:

| Tool | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `create_frame(title, description, position)` | Adds a topic-map frame |
| `create_note(text, near)` | Adds a text note next to a shape |
| `draw_arrow(from, to, label)` | Connects two shapes |
| `place_graph(spec, frame)` | Adds a `GraphShape` |
| `place_sim(type, params, frame)` | Adds a `SimShape` |
| `place_equation(latex, frame)` | Adds an `EquationShape` |
| `set_param(shape, key, value)` | Changes a parameter on a graph or simulation |
| `highlight(shape, part)` | Highlights a shape or a named part of it |
| `ask_prediction(shape, prompt)` | Asks the user to place a guess on a shape |
| `reply_in_thread(annotation, text)` | Answers an annotation in place |
| `render_animation(description, frame)` | Starts a background Manim job that adds a `VideoShape` when done |

**Model context.** Each call includes the shapes in and near the current view as JSON (type, props, position, frame), the selected objects, relevant annotation threads, the changes since the last call, and screenshots targeted at regions with freehand strokes or sketches. The JSON covers everything placed on the board and every parameter value.

**Models.** The backend is provider-agnostic: one interface over Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Argon, so the same session can be compared across models. A frontier model writes maps and new visualization code.

## Visualization (proposed)

The agent picks one of four ways to show something, from fastest to most flexible.

| Approach | Good for | How it is produced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catalog shapes | Graphs, standard simulations, equations | The model picks a shape and sets its props. Renders immediately |
| Declarative specs | Charts and diagrams | The model writes a Vega-Lite or Mermaid spec, rendered in a `SpecShape` |
| Generated code | Visuals no catalog shape covers | The model writes a small HTML and JS program that runs in a sandboxed iframe shape. It exposes its parameters and state through a typed bridge, so both sides can inspect and change it. It gets no access to the native bridge or the filesystem. A preview screenshot is checked, with a bounded number of repair attempts |
| Manim | Polished animations to keep. A low-resolution render and representative frames are reviewed for layout before the final render, and content correctness is checked separately | `render_animation`, in the background |

Pointing while talking comes from Clicky. Clicky's model appends a tag like `[POINT:x,y:label:screen2]` to its reply. The app strips the tag with a regex, sends the rest to text-to-speech, and flies a cursor in a transparent overlay to the coordinates along a curved path. Clicky needs pixel coordinates because it points at arbitrary apps. On the canvas every target has a shape or part ID, so tags reference those directly, for example `[HL:g1.curve]`. The first version points at the phrase level: a tag fires when its sentence starts playing. Word-level timing needs audio alignment, such as text-to-speech that streams character timestamps. The AI has its own visible cursor on the board that moves between targets.

## Annotations

An annotation is a mark plus a question. It is built in three steps: select and type, then mark and type, then mark and speak. Marks are made with the annotate tool, so ordinary drawing never starts listening or triggers the agent. Once mark and speak is in, listening starts as soon as an annotate stroke ends, so marking and speaking feel like one motion. The app shows which object it thinks the mark targets, and the user can correct it.

When a mark ends, the app takes the stroke's bounding box, finds the shapes it covers, and crops a screenshot of that region. The agent receives one object:

```json
{
  "annotation_id": "a_42",
  "stroke_type": "circle",
  "target_shape_ids": ["g1"],
  "target_detail": "GraphShape g1, y = x^2, near x = 2",
  "region_image": "<png>",
  "text": "why is the slope 4 here?"
}
```

The stroke binds to its target shapes with tldraw bindings, so moving or resizing a graph moves the circle and the AI's reply with it. If the target is deleted, the thread stays on the board, marked as detached. Each annotation is a thread: follow-up questions attach to it, and `reply_in_thread` answers there.

Stroke type sets the default intent when the user gives no text. A circle means explain this, an underline means go deeper, and a strike-through means the user thinks this is wrong. Any text or speech overrides the default.

## Voice

Voice comes in three steps: push-to-talk, then mark and speak, then hands-free conversation. It uses a realtime speech-to-speech API with tool calling over WebRTC in the browser. The voice model gets the same canvas tools as the agent, so it can talk while it highlights, sets parameters, or asks for a prediction. Work that needs a frontier model, such as building a map or writing a new visualization, goes through a `delegate` tool that calls the agent backend and returns when the shapes are on the board. When the user interrupts, speech stops and pending actions that are now obsolete are canceled.

The AI speaks and writes at the same time: short spoken explanations, with the durable content placed on the board as notes and shapes. A transcript of each exchange is stored with the board.

## macOS shell

The canvas stays a web app. The Mac app is a Swift shell that loads it in a `WKWebView` and adds what needs native APIs.

| Feature | Implementation | Permission |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Global hotkey (double tap of a modifier) | `CGEvent.tapCreate` on `flagsChanged`, about a 0.5 s window | Accessibility |
| Floating board window | Non-activating `NSPanel` | None |
| Screen capture mode | ScreenCaptureKit | Screen Recording |
| On-screen selection overlay | Transparent `NSPanel` over the active display | None |
| Microphone | `AVAudioEngine`, or `getUserMedia` inside the web view | Microphone |

The hotkey is configurable and defaults to double Right Option. Double Fn or Globe is the macOS default dictation shortcut, and double Control is one of the dictation alternatives.

**Screen capture mode.** The user presses the hotkey while reading anything on screen, such as a PDF or a lecture slide, and circles a region. The crop lands on the current board as an image shape with the user's question attached as an annotation.

**Bridge.** The web app sends messages to Swift through `WKScriptMessageHandler`. Swift calls into the web app with `evaluateJavaScript`. Messages are JSON with a `type` field, such as `capture_ready` or `open_board`.

The open-source Clicky code (MIT) is a reference for the hotkey, capture, and overlay.

## Storage

Everything is local, in one SQLite database.

| Table | Key fields |
| --- | --- |
| `commands` | `command_id, board_id, origin, type, payload, base_rev, status, created_at` |
| `boards` | `board_id`, `title`, `created_at`, `updated_at` |
| `snapshots` | `board_id`, `tldraw_snapshot`, `saved_at` |
| `annotations` | `annotation_id`, `board_id`, `stroke_type`, `target_shape_ids`, `text`, `created_at` |
| `thread_messages` | `annotation_id`, `author`, `text`, `created_at` |
| `transcripts` | `board_id`, `speaker`, `text`, `ts` |
| `renders` | `render_id`, `board_id`, `status`, `video_path`, `manim_source` |

Commands persist incrementally as they happen, and a full tldraw snapshot is saved periodically. The command log is the source for undo, revert, and replay. Manim output files live in the app's support directory, referenced by path.

## Build phases

Development starts as a web app on localhost in the browser. Phase 0 tests the product bet with a rough version before the foundation gets polished. Each later phase has a gate that must pass before the next starts.

0. **Rough loop, about two weeks.** tldraw agent starter, a simple command model, Ask with skeleton-then-fill, and select-and-type annotations. No styling work.\
**Gate:** run both test sessions and decide whether working this way beats chat.
1. **Paper canvas and typography.** Theme, rich text, frames, arrows, contextual controls, refined on a populated board.\
**Gate:** reading, selecting, editing, and navigating feel coherent with no AI involved.
2. **Commands, undo, and persistence.** Harden the command model: origin, stale-edit rejection, protected regions, cancel and revert, incremental persistence with periodic snapshots.\
**Gate:** reverting agent work never removes newer human work.
3. **Ask and progressive layout.** Full skeleton-then-fill, contextual placement, frame expansion, cancel and retry per frame. Asks can come by voice or text, with drawings and selections as context.
4. **Annotations and threads.** Select and type, then mark and type, then mark and speak. Inferred target shown and correctable. Bindings across move, resize, and delete.\
**Gate:** ordinary drawing never starts listening or triggers the agent.
5. **Sketching and handwriting.** Raw ink first, then explicit refine actions, with the original sketch recoverable. Test Apple Pencil, finger panning, and trackpad drawing here.\
**Gate:** switching between drawing, selecting, and editing never fights modes.
6. **Interactive objects.** KaTeX equations and native editable diagrams, then Mafs graphs, then one deterministic 2D simulation. D3 for layout, Three.js when content needs 3D.\
**Gate:** either participant changes a parameter and both see the same result.
7. **Predict and compare.** Predictions, sketches, and alternatives stored as board objects. Results appear next to the originals.\
**Gate:** the board preserves how an idea changed.
8. **Voice and pointing.** Push-to-talk, mark and speak, hands-free. Phrase-level pointing by shape and part ID.\
**Gate:** interrupting stops speech and obsolete actions.
9. **Context and proactive behavior.** Debounced checks, canceled on new interaction, ignoring agent-originated changes.\
**Gate:** no self-triggering loops and no interruptions during active work.
10. **Declarative and generated visuals.** Catalog objects, then Vega-Lite and Mermaid specs, then sandboxed generated widgets with the typed bridge.
11. **Manim and `VideoShape`.** Background rendering with progress, cancellation, cached outputs, and isolated jobs.
12. **Mac shell and screen capture.** `WKWebView` wrapper, hotkey, floating window, ScreenCaptureKit, with captures feeding the annotation flow.\
**Gate:** focus, multiple displays, and permissions work without a second interaction system.
13. **Cross-device.** iPad reconnect, shared-board updates, touch controls. Trusted HTTPS for microphone access on the local network.\
**Gate:** reconnecting never loses ink, annotations, or parameter changes.

The first complete milestone is phase 8. At that point people and agents can write, draw, annotate, manipulate, speak, and point together, and the combined experience gets refined before phases 9 to 13 add more systems.

Each change is tested on the two fixed sessions, one interaction at a time, comparing the old and new versions. Tracked: wrong targets, lost or overwritten edits, response latency, unnecessary interruptions, and which version is preferred.

## Open questions

- [ ] Realtime voice provider: OpenAI Realtime, Gemini Live, or a pipeline with character-timestamped text-to-speech

These are two separate layers. **Entire** is where Easel's repo lives and where changes get reviewed and merged. **Delta** shares and branches your live Claude Code sessions while you work.

## What each one does

| | Delta (Zed) | Entire |
|---|---|---|
| Role | Live session sync | Git forge (hosting, review, merge) |
| Captures | Every step between commits: messages, tool calls, and uncommitted files | Agent sessions recorded into Git history (the Checkpoints CLI), indexed for later recall |
| Key features | `/delta share`, `/delta join`, `delta thread fork`, `delta thread search` | Trails instead of PRs, review agents that score each push, Gates before merge |
| Git | Works on top of your Git checkout. You still commit as usual | A Git-compatible server, or a mirror of a GitHub repo |
| Cost and status | Beta, invite rollout | Hosting free at launch, review agents use tokens ($100 starter credit) |

## How I'd use them on Easel

**1. Set up the repo on Entire.** Either create it there, or keep it on GitHub and mirror it so GitHub stays the source of truth. Mirroring is the low-risk option while Entire is new. Commit the design doc as `docs/design.md`, plus a `CLAUDE.md` with the architecture decisions and your writing rules, so every session starts with the same context.

**2. One Trail per build phase.** Phase 0 (the rough loop) is a Trail, phase 1 is another, and so on. Set the gate for each to green CI (Vitest plus a Playwright smoke test of the board) and your approval.

**3. A custom review agent for Easel's own rules.** Entire lets you define review agents in a `.json` file in the repo. Write one that checks the command model, flagging any code that:

- changes the tldraw editor directly instead of going through a validated command,
- skips recording a command's origin, or
- writes into a protected user region.

These are the bugs most likely to break human and agent collaboration, and generic review won't catch them.

**4. Delta while you build.**

- **Switching machines:** `/delta share` on your laptop, `/delta join` from another machine, and you keep going with the full conversation and uncommitted changes.
- **Hill-climbing comparisons:** `delta thread fork` to try two versions of an interaction (say, mark-then-type against select-then-type) without touching the original thread. Keep the one that wins in your test sessions.
- **Testers:** share a thread so someone sees how a feature was built, or open it in the Delta app or browser.
- **History:** `delta thread search` to find why the agent made a decision weeks later.

**5. Memory across sessions.** Entire's entire-brain indexes recorded sessions against a local code map (entire-graph), so later agents can recall past decisions. Delta covers the session while it's live, and Entire covers what was decided afterward.

**One thing to watch:** both tools record sessions. Set Delta's recording policy (`/delta setup`) to manual, so you share on purpose instead of recording everything twice.

Day to day: write code in Claude Code with Delta running, push to a branch, let Entire's review agents score it on the Trail, fix findings, and merge when the gate is green.

# Grill-Me: Relentless Interactive Alignment Protocol

The goal of this skill is total alignment. Never assume requirements, invent unprompted deliverables, or begin writing code on underspecified prompts. Interrogate the design space first and force decisions to the surface.

---

## The Four-Phase Grilling Protocol

### Phase 1: Dissect the Request & Uncover Latent Forks

Before touching any code or creating files:
1. **Identify Unstated Assumptions:** What is the prompt taking for granted? What defaults are being assumed?
2. **Find Design Forks:** Are there two or more distinct ways to implement this? (e.g. In-memory vs persistent? CLI vs HTTP? Inline vs separate file?)
3. **Map Deliverable Boundaries:** What exact files should exist when the task finishes? What should NOT exist?
4. **Identify Integration Risks:** Does this break existing tests, CLI arguments, or persisted schemas?

---

### Phase 2: Interrogate with the `ask_question` Tool

Formulate structured, actionable multiple-choice questions using `ask_question`:

1. **Lead with (Recommended):** Put the recommended option first, clearly prefixed with `(Recommended)`.
2. **Make Choices Mutually Exclusive or Explicitly Multi-Select:** Each option should represent a distinct, concrete direction.
3. **Never Include "Other":** The tool automatically provides a write-in field.
4. **Format as User Direct Speech:** Frame options as direct user decisions (e.g., `"Build an interactive HTML codemap in docs/"`, not `"I will build..."`).
5. **No Trivial Questions:** Do not ask trivial yes/no questions that can be answered in text. Ask substantive architectural and scope questions.

---

### Phase 3: Bind to Specialized Global Skills

Every task must actively recruit the relevant global engineering skills:

- **Coding Standards (`coding-standards`):** Smallest complete change; self-explaining code; no speculative abstractions; preserve compatibility.
- **Technical Writing (`technical-writing`):** Diátaxis mode separation; Google developer style; Simplified Technical English (one thought per sentence); Global English syntax.
- **Verification Planning (`verification-planning` & `tdd`):** Test evidence planned before changing code; test at stable observable interfaces; narrowest checks first.
- **Visual Design (`design`):** Monochrome foundation first; high information density; zero emojis in technical docs and tools.
- **Bug Diagnosis (`diagnosing-bugs`):** Formulate hypotheses and inspect evidence before attempting speculative fixes.

---

### Phase 4: Confirm Boundaries & Plan

Once the user responds:
1. State the agreed deliverables and constraints explicitly.
2. Confirm the exact list of files to be created, modified, or deleted.
3. If uncertainty remains, ask a focused follow-up question.
4. Only proceed with execution once alignment is locked.

{"markdown":"[Skip to content](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code#main-content)

> **Beta:** The Claude Code plugin is in beta. Its behavior can change between
> releases.

Share a Claude Code conversation and its Git checkout with your Delta
organization, or with people you invite by email. A teammate can join the
shared thread from their own Claude Code session and continue the work.

The plugin runs the [Delta CLI](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/get-started) for you, so you don’t
need to learn its commands.

## [Quick start](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#quick-start)

### [1\. Install the plugin](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#1-install-the-plugin)

Everyone sharing or joining needs the plugin. In a terminal, first add the
Delta marketplace:

```
claude plugin marketplace add zed-industries/delta-claude
```

Then install the plugin from it:

```
claude plugin install delta@zed-industries
```

Start a new Claude Code session, or run `/reload-plugins` in one that’s
already open. Using the Claude desktop app? See
[Install in the Claude desktop app](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code#install-in-the-claude-desktop-app).

The plugin installs Delta for you the first time it needs it. On Windows, it
asks first: choose **Install Delta**.

> **Tip:** After you install the plugin, it offers to set up the repository.
> Choose **Set up now** to sync every conversation automatically. See
> [Set up automatic syncing](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code#set-up-automatic-syncing). To try sharing one
> conversation first, choose **Not now**.

### [2\. Share your conversation](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#2-share-your-conversation)

Open Claude Code in a Git checkout and run:

```
/delta share
```

Choose who should see the conversation. To share with your team, choose
**Share with** and your team’s name. If you don’t have a team, select **Type**
**something** and enter your teammate’s email address.

The first time, the plugin installs Delta if it’s missing and asks before
opening your browser to sign in. Once the conversation is shared, select
**copy link** and send the link to your teammate.

### [3\. Your teammate joins](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#3-your-teammate-joins)

Your teammate installs the plugin, starts a new Claude Code session in any
folder, and runs `/delta join` with your link:

```
/delta join https://delta.dev/join/thread_...
```

When Claude Code asks whether to trust the new folder, they choose **Yes, move**
**here**. Claude moves into a checkout of your files with the conversation as
context, and your teammate can continue the work.

## [Install in the Claude desktop app](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#install-in-the-claude-desktop-app)

1. In the Code tab, select **+** next to the prompt box, then **Add plugins**.
Typing `/plugin` in the prompt box opens the same screen.
2. Select **Add**, then **Add marketplace**.
3. Choose **Add from a repository**.
4. In **URL**, paste `https://github.com/zed-industries/delta-claude.git`,
then select **Sync**.
5. Under **Yours**, find **Delta** by Zed Industries and select **Add**.
6. Start a new session.

Installing the plugin in the desktop app also installs it for Claude Code in a
terminal, and the other way around.

To check that the plugin works, run `/delta` in the new session. The plugin
opens a menu of its actions, such as sharing this conversation or joining a
shared one.

## [Set up automatic syncing](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#set-up-automatic-syncing)

Once sharing works, set up the repository so you don’t need to run
`/delta share` in every session. Delta syncs each new conversation, and you
choose whether your team sees it.

1. Open Claude Code in the repository’s Git checkout and run `/delta setup`.
2. Choose the team conversations sync to. You can also create a team here, and
invite people to it by email. To keep conversations to yourself, choose
**Skip this step**.
3. Choose which sessions sync:
   - **Private sync:** every new session syncs, and only you can see it until
     you share it.
   - **Team sharing:** every new session is shared with your team.
   - **Manual:** sessions sync only when you run `/delta share`. This is how
     the plugin works until you set it up.

Setup saves your choice to `.delta/settings.json` at the checkout root and
keeps that file out of Git, so each teammate chooses for themselves. The
setting applies to new sessions, including ones started with `/clear`. After
saving, setup offers to sync your current session too.

You can also write the file yourself. `mode` is `manual`, `private`, or
`organization`, and `organization` is a team ID from `/delta org list`:

```
{
  "threads": {
    "mode": "private",
    "organization": "ORGANIZATION_ID"
  }
}
```

If the file isn’t valid, the plugin syncs nothing automatically and says
what’s wrong.

In a session that syncs automatically:

- To share a private conversation with your team, run `/delta share`.
- Claude keeps working offline. The conversation syncs when Delta reconnects.
- If Delta can’t sync your offline changes because a teammate changed the
thread, syncing pauses. Choose **Fork & Restore** to keep your changes in a
new thread, or **Discard** to drop them.

## [Share a conversation](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#share-a-conversation)

You can share at any point in a session, including before your first prompt.
If Claude is responding, wait for it to finish, then run `/delta share` and
choose who should see the conversation:

- **Share with** your team: everyone on the team can open it.
- **Just me (sync privately):** the conversation syncs, and only you can see
it. You can share it later.
- To invite specific people, select **Type something** and enter their email
addresses, separated by commas. Only you and the people you invite can open
the conversation.

To invite people without the question, add their addresses to the command:

```
/delta share ada@example.com sam@example.com
```

Sharing uses the team you chose when you
[set up the repository](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code#set-up-automatic-syncing), or your
selected team otherwise. After you share, the plugin keeps syncing new
activity in the session. A conversation that already syncs can’t become
private again, so the question offers **Keep current sharing** instead of
**Just me**.

### [What sharing includes](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#what-sharing-includes)

- Your messages and Claude’s replies, including thinking.
- Tool calls with their inputs and outputs.
- Images in the conversation.
- Your checkout’s files, including staged, unstaged, and untracked changes.

### [What sharing doesn’t include](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#what-sharing-doesnt-include)

- Prompt text you haven’t sent.
- Files Git ignores, such as build output, and local Git state such as branches.
- Extra folders you added with `--add-dir`.
- Earlier Claude sessions, and messages that compaction removed. The plugin
exports up to the newest 4,096 messages of the current conversation.

## [Join a conversation](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#join-a-conversation)

1. Start a new Claude Code session. Any folder works, because joining moves
Claude into the thread’s files.
2. Run `/delta join` with the link you received. The link’s last part,
starting with `thread_`, also works on its own.
3. When Claude asks whether to trust the new folder, choose **Yes, move here**.
**No, stay put** pauses the join until you run `/delta join` again.
4. Once the join finishes, send your next prompt.

To join, you need to be on the thread’s team or invited to the thread.
Joining starts a fresh Claude session in a checkout of the thread’s files that
Delta creates. Your previous session and folder stay as they were, and you can
resume that session later. Joining doesn’t add your previous conversation to
the thread or start a Claude turn.

You can also join from an existing session. Claude must be idle, with no
background agents or agent team members running.

> **Tip:** In the Delta app, open a shared thread and choose **Edit > Open in**
> **Claude Code**. Claude Code opens with `/delta join` and the link already
> typed.

### [Work in a joined conversation](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#work-in-a-joined-conversation)

The joined session gets the thread’s conversation as context. It’s a new
Claude session, not a copy of the original one. For long threads, Claude gets
the most recent messages, plus a note explaining how to read older ones with
`delta thread show`. The transcript shows only the latest few messages when
you join.

While you’re connected:

- Messages from teammates appear in your transcript but don’t start a Claude
turn. Claude sees them with your next prompt.
- Comments made in Delta reach Claude once someone sends them with a message.
- Another agent’s thinking appears in your transcript, but Claude doesn’t
receive it.

checkout. With several, Claude works in a folder containing a link to each
one. The plugin blocks prompts until every checkout is ready.

When you exit a joined session, Delta uploads your changes and then deletes
its checkouts. Ignored files, such as build output, and local Git branches are
deleted with them, so don’t keep anything there that you need later.

A team is a Delta organization, the same one you see in the Delta app.

```
/delta org list
/delta org current
/delta org switch ORGANIZATION_ID
/delta org invite ada@example.com sam@example.com
/delta org manage
```

- `list` shows your teams and their IDs, and `current` shows the selected one.
- `switch` selects a different team. Repositories you set up keep the team you
chose in setup.
- `invite` invites people to the selected team. Members can open every
conversation shared with the team. To give someone access to one
conversation only, use [`/delta share`](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code#share-a-conversation) with their
email address.
- `manage` opens the team’s members page in your browser.

To create a team in the Delta app, open the user menu and choose **Create**
**Organization**, which opens the form on dashboard.zed.dev. See
[Create an organization](https://delta.dev/docs/account/authenticate#create-an-organization).

## [Update Delta](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#update-delta)

When Claude Code starts, the plugin tells you if a newer Delta is available.
To install it, run `/delta update`. A running Delta app restarts to install the
update. Your synced and shared sessions disconnect briefly and reconnect on
their own. On Windows, approve the Windows prompt if one appears.
If an agent turn or a background terminal is running in Delta, nothing is
stopped: run `/delta update` again once the work finishes.

## [Update the plugin](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#update-the-plugin)

The plugin checks for a newer version of itself once an hour and offers to
update. To update it yourself, run `/delta plugin-update`. To turn the checks
off, run `/delta plugin-update notifications off`, and
`/delta plugin-update notifications on` turns them back on. Checks need Claude
Code’s `claude` command on your `PATH`.

## [Troubleshooting](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#troubleshooting)

**The plugin says Delta is too old:** the plugin reuses a Delta that’s
already installed, even an old one. Update it from the Delta app with
**Delta > Check for Updates**, then run your command again.

**The plugin says Delta is newer than the plugin:** run
`/delta plugin-update`, then run your command again.

**Sharing failed:** fix the problem Delta reports, then run
`/delta share` again in the same session. If the conversation already syncs,
choose **Keep current sharing** to reconnect it without changing who can see
it.

**An automatic sync failed:** fix the problem Delta reports and send your next
prompt. The plugin tries again.

**Joining failed, or you chose No, stay put:** run `/delta join` again with
the same link. It continues where it stopped.

**A joined session disconnected:** run `/delta join` again with the same link.
It reconnects without starting another new session. In a joined session,
always recover with `/delta join`, not `/delta share`.

**You resumed a joined session:** wait for the plugin to restore the checkouts
and move Claude back to them. Prompts are blocked until then.

## [Requirements](https://delta.dev/docs/cli/claude-code\#requirements)

- Claude Code 2.1.303 or newer, in a terminal or the Code tab of the Claude
desktop app. Older versions show a warning, and some features may not work.
Plugins are enabled by default, but your company’s Claude Code policy can
turn them off.
- Delta 0.22.0 or newer.
- To share: a Git checkout with a remote. If the repository has several
remotes, one must be named `origin`.
- To join: membership in the thread’s team, or an invitation to the thread.

The plugin doesn’t support Claude Code cloud sessions, print mode
(`claude -p`), or SDK sessions yet.

| `/delta` | Open a menu of the plugin’s actions |

| `/delta setup` | Choose this repository’s team and which sessions sync |

| `/delta org current` | Show the selected team |
| `/delta org switch ID` | Select a different team |
| `/delta org invite EMAIL…` | Invite people to the selected team |
| `/delta org manage` | Open the team’s members page in your browser |

# Technical writing

The goal is writing a tired engineer understands on the first read. Four layers get you there, one question each: what kind of document is this, how do sentences address the reader, how much does each sentence carry, and can any sentence be read two ways. Apply all four.

Three rules sit above the layers:

- **Cut every word that does no work.** If the sentence survives without a word, the word goes. "In order to" is "to". "It is important to note that" is nothing.
- **Use the short, everyday word.** "Use", not "utilize". "Help", not "facilitate". "Do", not "perform". A long word has to buy its length with precision.
- **When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.** The rules serve the reader. A sentence that follows every rule and sounds like a machine wrote it has failed.

The codebase is the word list. Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it.

Don't invent jargon. Use the words a developer would say out loud: "move", "delete", "a budget that only decreases", not "evacuate", "ratchet", or "endgame". A named pattern is fine when the doc says what it means the first time. Add new offenders and their replacements to rule 26 in `references/unslop.md`.

## Vary the rhythm

The layers decide what a document says and how much each sentence carries. A doc can obey all of them and still read machine-written: every sentence clipped short, no view anywhere, nothing specific.

- Mix sentence lengths on purpose. Short sentences land a point. Longer ones that take their time carry a fact with its condition or consequence.
- One thought per sentence does not mean one length per sentence. Split the sentence that carries two thoughts. Keep the long sentence that carries one.
- Have a view where the mode allows it. Explanation weighs trade-offs, so say what you make of them instead of listing pros and cons. Reference stays dry.
- Be specific over sterile. Not "schema changes can cause issues" but "a column rename fails the build".

## Pick the mode first (Diátaxis)

One document, one mode. For a ground-up tutorial, study guide, or cheat sheet that teaches a domain from its smallest unit, use the textbook mode in `references/textbook.md` instead. Two questions pick the Diátaxis mode: does the content inform action (doing) or understanding (thinking), and does it serve learning or work?

- Action + learning: **tutorial**.
- Action + work: **how-to**.
- Understanding + work: **reference**.
- Understanding + learning: **explanation**.

Use the compass on a whole document or on one sentence. Reach for it whenever you feel unsure what you are writing. Gut feel is often wrong here.

**Tutorial: learning by doing.** You are the teacher. The learner's success is your job, not theirs. Open by saying what the learner will build, not what they will "learn". Every step produces a visible result, early and often. Tell them what they should see: the expected output, the prompt change, the log line. Cut explanation to one clause and a link. Teaching pauses break the lesson. Stay concrete. Write as "we", in commands: "First, do x. Now, do y."

**How-to: steps to a goal.** Solve a problem a person has, not an operation the machine can perform. Assume competence. Skip teaching. Action only: no digressions, no background, no completeness for its own sake. Link those instead. Allow forks and judgment: "If you want x, do y." Name the guide by the task: "How to calibrate the radar array", not "Radar array calibration".

**Reference: facts for lookup.** Describe. Only describe. No instruction, no persuasion, no opinion. Be dry, complete, and sure: state facts, options, limits, and errors with no hedging. Mirror the structure of the thing described, so code and docs can be navigated together. Put material where readers expect it. Generate from code where possible, so it stays true.

**Explanation: understanding and why.** One bounded topic, readable away from the product. Each title should tolerate an implicit "About..." in front. Anchor on a real why question. Give context: design decisions, history, constraints, alternatives. Opinion is allowed here and nowhere else.

Don't mix modes: no reference tables inside a tutorial, no tutorial hand-holding inside reference, no arguing inside a how-to. Split and link instead.

Source: diataxis.fr, fetched 2026-07-18.

## Write sentences to the reader (Google developer style)

- Talk to the reader as "you", in the present tense. "Will" only for things that genuinely happen later.
- Say who does what: "the compiler checks", not "is checked". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or beside the point.
- Write instructions as commands: "Click Submit." State facts plainly. Never "should be done".
- Put the condition before the instruction: "To delete the document, click Delete." The reader skips what does not apply.
- Put the common case first. Exceptions after.
- Sound like a knowledgeable friend. No buzzwords, no figurative language, no "please" in instructions, and never "simply", "easy", or "quickly" in a procedure. If it were simple, the reader would not be here.
- Don't pre-announce ("we will soon support...") and don't start consecutive sentences with the same phrase.
- Read the awkward sentence aloud. If it stays awkward, rewrite it.
- Link with words that say where the link goes: the page title or a short description. Never "click here". Prefer a sentence of context on the page over a link off it.
- Headings carry the point, not just the topic ("Pick the mode first", not "Modes"). Sentence case. A task heading is a bare verb phrase ("Create an instance"). A concept heading is a noun phrase. One h1 per page, no skipped levels.
- Numbered lists for sequences, bullets for everything else. Introduce a list with a complete sentence. Keep items parallel.
- Code goes in code font. UI elements go in bold. Use serial commas. Drop "etc." and say up front that a list is partial.

Source: developers.google.com/style, fetched 2026-07-18.

## Make statements load one at a time (STE rules)

- One instruction per sentence. One thought per sentence everywhere else.
- Split instructions longer than about 20 words and other sentences longer than about 25.
- Put the warning or condition before the step it guards: "If hot oil touches your skin, injuries can occur."
- Keep "the" and "a": "Remove backup file" reads two ways. "Remove the backup file" reads one.
- Give each word one meaning and one job, then keep it. If "check" means inspect, don't also use it for restrain.
- Pick one word per action and stick to it: "start", not "start" here and "initiate" there.
- Write procedures as direct commands, never as narration and never in the passive: "Install the component", not "the component must be installed".
- Avoid "-ing" words where you can. They take too many grammatical jobs and breed misreadings.

Source: asd-ste100.org (Issue 9, 2025), fetched 2026-07-18. The numbered rules and dictionary live in the spec PDF. The principles above are the transferable core.

## Leave no sentence open to two readings (Global English)

- Keep words like "only" and "not" next to the word they change: "only fails on growth" and "fails only on growth" say different things.
- Break up long noun strings: "the proto import budget check script" becomes "the script that checks the proto-import budget".
- Make every "it", "they", and "this" point at one obvious thing. Repeat the noun when in doubt. Never use "this" or "which" to point at a whole clause.
- Don't drop verbs: "Phase 1 moves the converters and Phase 2 the runtime" leaves Phase 2 without one. Give it one.
- Keep the small words that show structure. "Ensure that the switch is off" keeps "that" because it makes the sentence parse one way. Never trade clarity for word count.
- Repeat the article in a series when it prevents a misread: "the client and the host", not "the client and host", when they are two things.
- Say which parts "and" or "or" joins when a sentence can group two ways. "Both...and", "either...or", and "if...then" are free disambiguators.
- Use periods, not semicolons. Replace an em dash with a new sentence.
- Make text in parentheses a full grammatical unit or its own sentence. Never form plurals with "(s)".
- No slashes: write "a, b, or both" instead of "a/b" or "and/or".
- Call each thing by one name, everywhere. A doc that says "the gate", "the ratchet", and "the budget check" for one thing teaches three things. Rewording an unchanged sentence between edits costs the same way: don't churn what didn't change.
- Skip idioms, colloquialisms, Latin abbreviations, and metaphors. A non-native reader, a translator, and an agent all parse plain constructions best.

Source: Kohl, The Global English Style Guide (SAS Press). Guideline text fetched from the Internet Archive and the SAS sample chapter, 2026-07-18.

## Voice and repo specifics

- Apply `references/unslop.md` to every doc this skill touches. It owns the slop-pattern catalog: AI vocabulary, filler, hedging, and formatting tells. For a request to only de-slop some text, apply that catalog alone and keep the author's structure.
- PR descriptions and commit messages are writing too. Every layer except Diátaxis applies to them.
- Product UI strings are not documentation. Use your product's copy guidelines for those.
- Indent code snippets with tabs. Write real paths and real symbols. Make every count or tree claim true at the commit that lands it, and include the command that regenerates it.

## Worked example

Before:

> Configuration of the proto import ratchet budget script parameters is performed via budget.json. Note that it's important to remember that running with --write, which updates the committed budget to reflect the current count, should only be done when lowering it. If exceeded, CI fails.

After:

> `budget.mjs` reads the committed budget from `budget.json` and counts the files that import protos. If the count exceeds the budget, CI fails. Run `budget.mjs --write` only to lower the budget.

The fixes, by layer: "configuration is performed" becomes "`budget.mjs` reads", so someone does something (Google). "Ratchet" goes away. The script's real filename does the naming (jargon rule). The five-noun string breaks up into plain clauses (Global English). The hedge "note that it's important to remember" is deleted (cut every word that does no work). The failure condition moves ahead of the step it explains (STE). The buried "should only be done when lowering" becomes a command with "only" next to its verb (STE). "If exceeded" gets a subject: the count (Global English).

## Review checklist

Apply to any prose this skill covers. Item 1 applies only to document sets:

1. Is each file one Diátaxis mode, with links where modes meet?
2. Is every instruction written as a command, with its condition in front?
3. Does any sentence carry two instructions or two thoughts? Split it.
4. Can any word be cut without losing meaning? Cut it.
5. Is "only" next to the word it changes? Does every "it" point at one thing? Does every clause keep its verb?
6. Does each thing have exactly one name across the docs?
7. Would a developer say these words out loud? Replace invented metaphors and fancy synonyms with the plain word or the real symbol name.
8. Are all symbols, paths, and counts real at this commit, with the commands that regenerate the counts?

Reference for writing any document an agent consumes — a skill, an `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`, a doc reached by a pointer. The packaging differs; the writing does not: the same levers make each one predictable — the agent taking the same _process_ every run, not producing the same output.

When the document you're writing is a skill, read [`SKILL-MECHANICS.md`](SKILL-MECHANICS.md) for frontmatter, invocation choice, and router skills.

## Context pointers

A **context pointer** is a reference held in the agent's context that names some out-of-context material and encodes the condition for reaching it. A skill's description is one; a line in `AGENTS.md` naming a doc is the same object. The pointer's _wording_, not its target, decides when the agent reaches the material — and how reliably. A must-have target behind a weakly worded pointer is a variance bug: sharpen the wording first, and inline the material only if sharpening fails.

A pointer does two jobs — state what the material is, and list the **branches** that should trigger reaching it (a branch is a distinct case the document handles, so different runs take different paths through it). Every word of an always-loaded pointer costs on every turn, so it earns even harder pruning than the body:

- **Front-load the leading word** — the pointer is where it does its triggering work.
- **One trigger per branch.** Synonyms that rename a single branch are one branch written twice; collapse them and keep only genuinely distinct branches.
- **Cut identity the body already carries.**

## The two loads

Every document and pointer you add spends one of two budgets:

- **Context load** — the cost of always-loaded material on the agent's window: an `AGENTS.md` line, a skill description, anything sitting in context every turn, spending tokens and attention whether or not it fires.
- **Cognitive load** — the cost on the human: which documents exist and when to reach for each. The human is the index. Not a cost to minimise — it is the price of human agency; spend it where human judgement matters, remove it where it does not.

Material reached only through a pointer escapes context load at the price of the pointer's own line; material with no pointer at all rides entirely on cognitive load.

## Information hierarchy

A document is built from two content types — **steps** (the ordered actions the agent performs) and **reference** (definitions, rules, facts consulted on demand) — that mix freely: all steps (a recipe), all reference (a review's rules, this skill), or both. The core decision is where each piece sits on the **information hierarchy**, a ladder ranked by how immediately the agent needs the material:

1. **In-file step** — the primary tier: what the agent does, in order.
2. **In-file reference** — consulted on demand. Often a legitimately flat peer-set (every rule of a review on one rung) — a fine arrangement, not a smell.
3. **Disclosed reference** — pushed out into a separate file, reached by a context pointer, loaded only when the pointer fires. Spans a sibling file in the same folder through fully external reference that lives anywhere and any document can point at.

Push too little down and the top bloats; push too much and you hide material the agent actually needs. That tension is the whole decision.

**Progressive disclosure** is the move down the ladder — out of the main file and behind a pointer — so the top stays legible. Not primarily a token optimisation: it is how the hierarchy is protected. Branching is the cleanest disclosure test: inline what every branch needs, and push behind a pointer what only some branches reach. When a document has steps, in-file reference that should be disclosed buries them and turns attending to them into a coin-flip — a variance lever, not just a legibility one.

**Co-location** is the within-file companion: where the ladder decides _how far down_ a piece sits, co-location decides _what sits beside it_ once there. Keep a concept's definition, rules, and caveats under one heading rather than scattered, so reading one part brings its neighbours with it. The test: the document should read like documentation written for the agent — grouped material reads that way; scattered material does not. (Distinct from duplication: that repeats one meaning in two places; scattering fragments one meaning across many.)

**Sprawl** is the failure mode here: a document simply too long, even when every line is live and unique. Attention thins across the excess, and every extra line is one more to keep relevant. The cure is the ladder: disclose reference behind pointers, and split by branch or sequence so each path carries only what it needs.

## Steps and completion criteria

Every step ends on a **completion criterion** — the condition that tells the agent the work is done. Two properties make it a lever:

- **Clarity** — can the agent tell done from not-done? A vague bound ("understanding reached") invites **premature completion**: ending the step before it is genuinely done, attention slipping to _being done_. The visible steps still ahead — the **post-completion steps** — supply the pull; the criterion's clarity is the resistance. Defend in order: **sharpen the bound first** (local and cheap); only if it is irreducibly fuzzy _and_ you observe the rush, hide the later steps by splitting the sequence — and hiding only works across a real context boundary (a hand-off or a subagent dispatch; an inline call leaves the later steps in context and clears nothing).
- **Demand** — how much it requires. "Every modified model accounted for" forces thorough work where "produce a change list" does not. Demand drives **legwork** — the digging the agent does within the work, latent in the wording rather than written as its own step — and it is not step-bound: "every rule applied" binds a body of flat reference just as "every step done" binds a sequence, which is how an all-reference document still carries an exhaustiveness bar.

The strongest criteria are both checkable and exhaustive.

## When to split

Splitting one document into two spends one of the two loads, so split only when the cut earns it:

- **By sequence** — split a run of steps where the post-completion steps tempt the agent to rush the one in front of it. Keeping them out of view drives more legwork on the current task. Beware the reverse: merging sequences exposes each step's later steps to what follows, inviting premature completion.
- **By invocation** — skill-specific: see [`SKILL-MECHANICS.md`](SKILL-MECHANICS.md).

## Leading words

A **leading word** is a compact concept already living in the model's pretraining that the agent thinks with while running the document (_lesson_, _fog of war_, _tracer bullets_). Repeated as a token, never as a sentence, it accumulates a distributed definition and anchors a whole region of behaviour in the fewest tokens, by recruiting priors the model already holds. Coining your own works if you define it clearly, but a made-up word recruits no priors — you pay in definition tokens what a pretrained word gives free; reach for an existing word first.

It anchors twice. In the body, _execution_: the agent reaches for the same behaviour every time the word appears, and inside flat reference it focuses attention on a class of thing to look for. In a pointer, _invocation_: when the same word lives in your prompts, your docs, and your codebase, the agent links that shared language to the material and reaches it more reliably.

Hunt for opportunities to refactor with leading words. A triad spelled out at three sites, a pointer spending a sentence to gesture at one idea — each is a passage begging to collapse into a single token:

- "fast, deterministic, low-overhead" → _tight_ (a _tight_ loop).
- "a loop you believe in" → _red_ — a fuzzy gate becomes a binary observable state (the loop goes _red_ on the bug, or it doesn't).

You win twice: fewer tokens, and a sharper hook for the agent to hang its thinking on. Assume every document is carrying restatements that leading words retire — go find them.

**Negation** is the failure mode beside this lever: steering by prohibition drags the forbidden behaviour into context and makes it _more_ available, not less. _Don't think of an elephant_, and the elephant is all there is; the negation is a weak modifier the strongly-activated concept overruns, so the ban half-reads as an instruction to do the thing. Prompt the **positive** — state the target behaviour ("write one-line comments") so the banned one is never spoken. A prohibition earns its place only as a hard guardrail you cannot phrase positively; even then, pair it with the positive target so attention lands on what to do.

## Pruning

- Keep each meaning in a **single source of truth**: one authoritative place, so changing the behaviour is a one-place edit. **Duplication** — the same meaning in more than one place — costs maintenance and tokens, and inflates a meaning's prominence on the ladder past its real rank. (The accidental inverse of a leading word, which repeats a token on purpose, never the meaning.)
- The **environment** is a source of truth too — `package.json` scripts, config files, the directory layout, `--help` output — and a document that restates it is a **cache**: a copy of a lookup, earning its load only when the lookup is expensive. Cache what the agent cannot find by looking: the unwritten convention, the reason behind a choice, the gotcha no config confesses. Leave the one-file, one-command lookups to the environment, where they cannot go stale.
- Check every line for **relevance**: does it still bear on what the document does? A line loses relevance by never bearing on the task (mere exposition, or a branch that should be disclosed) or by going stale as the behaviour or world it describes changes. Shorter documents are easier to keep relevant. Without a pruning discipline the default fate is **sediment**: stale layers that settle because adding feels safe and removing feels risky, until you must core down through them to find what is still live.
- Hunt **no-ops** sentence by sentence: an instruction the model already obeys by default pays load to say nothing. The test — does it change behaviour versus the default? — is model-relative, not reader-relative: two people disagreeing about a no-op disagree about the default, and settle it by running the document, not by debate. When a sentence fails, delete the whole sentence rather than trim words from it. The test also grades leading words: a word too weak to beat the default (_be thorough_ when the agent is already thorough-ish) is a no-op, and the fix is a stronger word (_relentless_), not a different technique.

# Easel

Oct 31, 2026 · @Guy-robert

## Product direction

A shared multimodal canvas where people and agents explore, create, and revise ideas together. Learning a technical topic, planning a project, building a mockup, and brainstorming are all uses of the same collaboration model, so the product is not limited to one subject or to tutoring.

The bet is that people prefer working with agents this way over chat. Individual features do not need to be novel. What matters is the quality of continuous collaboration: both participants work on the same objects, and text, voice, ink, and comments all change the same board state.

Two repeatable sessions are the test bed for every change: exploring a physics concept and developing a project mockup.

## Interaction model

The user and the AI work on one infinite canvas. Both act through the same set of primitives, and every action changes shared board state that the other side can see.

| Primitive | User | AI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ask | Types or speaks with nothing selected | Asks the user a question, by voice or as a note |
| Annotate | Circles, underlines, or highlights an element, then types or speaks about it | Highlights an element and attaches a note or arrow to it |
| Manipulate | Drags a slider, moves an object, changes a parameter | Sets parameters on graphs and simulations |
| Sketch | Draws a freehand diagram or curve | Turns a sketch into a precise shape |
| Predict | Places a guess before a result is shown | Requests a prediction, then reveals the result next to it |

The AI acts when the user addresses it by voice or text. It may also act after the user pauses: a change on the board starts a debounce of about 1.5 s, any new user interaction cancels the pending check, and changes the agent made itself never start one. When the check runs, staying quiet is a valid outcome.

## Board layout

One board per topic or project. When the user asks for something, the AI first places a map: a row of empty tldraw frames, one per part, each with a title and a one-line description of what it will hold. For Fourier transforms that might be intuition, the math, a worked example, and applications. For a mockup it might be goals, user flow, screens, and open decisions. The AI then fills the frames one at a time, so the user can start working in the first frame while later ones are still being generated. The user can cancel or retry generation per frame.

The area to the left of the map is the user's space for scratch work, drawings, and their own notes. Protected regions are enforced in code: agent commands that target them are rejected unless the user asked for that change. New AI content goes next to the frame it relates to, and the user's camera stays where it is while the agent adds content elsewhere.

The user can ask the AI to add a frame, split one into smaller parts, or go deeper on one part. Each of those runs the same skeleton-then-fill process on a smaller scope.

## Architecture

[embedded content: Components and how they connect]

The Swift shell handles the hotkey and screen capture and hosts the web app. The canvas and the voice model both change the board through the agent backend's canvas tools. The backend calls a frontier model for topic maps and new visualizations, and runs Manim jobs in the background.

## Canvas and shapes

The canvas is the current tldraw SDK (5.6.0 on npm as of November 2) in a React app, starting from the tldraw agent starter kit at the matching version. Reuse the starter's context collection, validated actions, streaming, and cancellation, and extend its shape schemas so the agent can read and edit custom parameters. tldraw is free on localhost. Shipping it, including inside a desktop app, requires a tldraw license key.

Built-in tldraw shapes cover notes, text, arrows, frames, highlights, and freehand strokes. Interactive content uses custom shapes that host React components:

| Shape | Renders with | Parameters both sides can set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GraphShape` | Mafs or JSXGraph | Function, domain, marked points, sliders |
| `SimShape` | Three.js with a physics step in code | Simulation type and its parameters, such as launch angle and initial velocity |
| `EquationShape` | KaTeX | LaTeX source, highlighted terms |
| `DiagramShape` | D3 | Nodes, edges, layout |
| `VideoShape` | HTML video | Source file from a Manim render |

Each custom shape stores its parameters in tldraw shape props, so a change from either side is a normal board update and syncs to everything else that reads the board.

Shapes expose stable shape and part IDs, such as `g1.curve` or `eq3.term2`, so annotations, pointing, and agent commands can target parts of a shape.

### Visual direction

The board should feel like paper: warm paper tones, dark ink, an editorial serif for prose, a clean sans-serif for controls, generous spacing, and low surface contrast. Content looks typeset onto the canvas, and frames organize it quietly instead of enclosing everything in cards or sticky notes. Selection outlines and contextual controls appear when needed, and permanent interface chrome stays small. Body text starts around 17 to 18 px at reading zoom. Source Serif 4 is a candidate for the serif, to be compared against reference typography before it is chosen. Text wrapping, selection, equation alignment, and editing get refined before decorative motion. tldraw custom themes and rich text cover most of this.

## Agent and canvas tools

The agent backend is a local TypeScript process that shares shape schemas and the command model with the frontend. Every board change, from the UI or the agent, is a validated command, so there is one code path for every change.

- Each command records its origin: user, agent, or voice.
- Dragging and other direct manipulation apply locally and immediately. The command is recorded after the fact.
- Agent commands carry the board revision they were based on. A command whose target changed since then is rejected as stale.
- Commands into protected user regions are rejected.
- Cancel stops future agent work. Revert is a separate action, and reverting agent work never removes newer human work.

The agent's tools are commands:

| Tool | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `create_frame(title, description, position)` | Adds a topic-map frame |
| `create_note(text, near)` | Adds a text note next to a shape |
| `draw_arrow(from, to, label)` | Connects two shapes |
| `place_graph(spec, frame)` | Adds a `GraphShape` |
| `place_sim(type, params, frame)` | Adds a `SimShape` |
| `place_equation(latex, frame)` | Adds an `EquationShape` |
| `set_param(shape, key, value)` | Changes a parameter on a graph or simulation |
| `highlight(shape, part)` | Highlights a shape or a named part of it |
| `ask_prediction(shape, prompt)` | Asks the user to place a guess on a shape |
| `reply_in_thread(annotation, text)` | Answers an annotation in place |
| `render_animation(description, frame)` | Starts a background Manim job that adds a `VideoShape` when done |

**Model context.** Each call includes the shapes in and near the current view as JSON (type, props, position, frame), the selected objects, relevant annotation threads, the changes since the last call, and screenshots targeted at regions with freehand strokes or sketches. The JSON covers everything placed on the board and every parameter value.

**Models.** The backend is provider-agnostic: one interface over Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Argon, so the same session can be compared across models. A frontier model writes maps and new visualization code.

## Visualization (proposed)

The agent picks one of four ways to show something, from fastest to most flexible.

| Approach | Good for | How it is produced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catalog shapes | Graphs, standard simulations, equations | The model picks a shape and sets its props. Renders immediately |
| Declarative specs | Charts and diagrams | The model writes a Vega-Lite or Mermaid spec, rendered in a `SpecShape` |
| Generated code | Visuals no catalog shape covers | The model writes a small HTML and JS program that runs in a sandboxed iframe shape. It exposes its parameters and state through a typed bridge, so both sides can inspect and change it. It gets no access to the native bridge or the filesystem. A preview screenshot is checked, with a bounded number of repair attempts |
| Manim | Polished animations to keep. A low-resolution render and representative frames are reviewed for layout before the final render, and content correctness is checked separately | `render_animation`, in the background |

Pointing while talking comes from Clicky. Clicky's model appends a tag like `[POINT:x,y:label:screen2]` to its reply. The app strips the tag with a regex, sends the rest to text-to-speech, and flies a cursor in a transparent overlay to the coordinates along a curved path. Clicky needs pixel coordinates because it points at arbitrary apps. On the canvas every target has a shape or part ID, so tags reference those directly, for example `[HL:g1.curve]`. The first version points at the phrase level: a tag fires when its sentence starts playing. Word-level timing needs audio alignment, such as text-to-speech that streams character timestamps. The AI has its own visible cursor on the board that moves between targets.

## Annotations

An annotation is a mark plus a question. It is built in three steps: select and type, then mark and type, then mark and speak. Marks are made with the annotate tool, so ordinary drawing never starts listening or triggers the agent. Once mark and speak is in, listening starts as soon as an annotate stroke ends, so marking and speaking feel like one motion. The app shows which object it thinks the mark targets, and the user can correct it.

When a mark ends, the app takes the stroke's bounding box, finds the shapes it covers, and crops a screenshot of that region. The agent receives one object:

```json
{
  "annotation_id": "a_42",
  "stroke_type": "circle",
  "target_shape_ids": ["g1"],
  "target_detail": "GraphShape g1, y = x^2, near x = 2",
  "region_image": "<png>",
  "text": "why is the slope 4 here?"
}
```

The stroke binds to its target shapes with tldraw bindings, so moving or resizing a graph moves the circle and the AI's reply with it. If the target is deleted, the thread stays on the board, marked as detached. Each annotation is a thread: follow-up questions attach to it, and `reply_in_thread` answers there.

Stroke type sets the default intent when the user gives no text. A circle means explain this, an underline means go deeper, and a strike-through means the user thinks this is wrong. Any text or speech overrides the default.

## Voice

Voice comes in three steps: push-to-talk, then mark and speak, then hands-free conversation. It uses a realtime speech-to-speech API with tool calling over WebRTC in the browser. The voice model gets the same canvas tools as the agent, so it can talk while it highlights, sets parameters, or asks for a prediction. Work that needs a frontier model, such as building a map or writing a new visualization, goes through a `delegate` tool that calls the agent backend and returns when the shapes are on the board. When the user interrupts, speech stops and pending actions that are now obsolete are canceled.

The AI speaks and writes at the same time: short spoken explanations, with the durable content placed on the board as notes and shapes. A transcript of each exchange is stored with the board.

## macOS shell

The canvas stays a web app. The Mac app is a Swift shell that loads it in a `WKWebView` and adds what needs native APIs.

| Feature | Implementation | Permission |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Global hotkey (double tap of a modifier) | `CGEvent.tapCreate` on `flagsChanged`, about a 0.5 s window | Accessibility |
| Floating board window | Non-activating `NSPanel` | None |
| Screen capture mode | ScreenCaptureKit | Screen Recording |
| On-screen selection overlay | Transparent `NSPanel` over the active display | None |
| Microphone | `AVAudioEngine`, or `getUserMedia` inside the web view | Microphone |

The hotkey is configurable and defaults to double Right Option. Double Fn or Globe is the macOS default dictation shortcut, and double Control is one of the dictation alternatives.

**Screen capture mode.** The user presses the hotkey while reading anything on screen, such as a PDF or a lecture slide, and circles a region. The crop lands on the current board as an image shape with the user's question attached as an annotation.

**Bridge.** The web app sends messages to Swift through `WKScriptMessageHandler`. Swift calls into the web app with `evaluateJavaScript`. Messages are JSON with a `type` field, such as `capture_ready` or `open_board`.

The open-source Clicky code (MIT) is a reference for the hotkey, capture, and overlay.

## Storage

Everything is local, in one SQLite database.

| Table | Key fields |
| --- | --- |
| `commands` | `command_id, board_id, origin, type, payload, base_rev, status, created_at` |
| `boards` | `board_id`, `title`, `created_at`, `updated_at` |
| `snapshots` | `board_id`, `tldraw_snapshot`, `saved_at` |
| `annotations` | `annotation_id`, `board_id`, `stroke_type`, `target_shape_ids`, `text`, `created_at` |
| `thread_messages` | `annotation_id`, `author`, `text`, `created_at` |
| `transcripts` | `board_id`, `speaker`, `text`, `ts` |
| `renders` | `render_id`, `board_id`, `status`, `video_path`, `manim_source` |

Commands persist incrementally as they happen, and a full tldraw snapshot is saved periodically. The command log is the source for undo, revert, and replay. Manim output files live in the app's support directory, referenced by path.

## Build phases

Development starts as a web app on localhost in the browser. Phase 0 tests the product bet with a rough version before the foundation gets polished. Each later phase has a gate that must pass before the next starts.

0. **Rough loop, about two weeks.** tldraw agent starter, a simple command model, Ask with skeleton-then-fill, and select-and-type annotations. No styling work.\
**Gate:** run both test sessions and decide whether working this way beats chat.
1. **Paper canvas and typography.** Theme, rich text, frames, arrows, contextual controls, refined on a populated board.\
**Gate:** reading, selecting, editing, and navigating feel coherent with no AI involved.
2. **Commands, undo, and persistence.** Harden the command model: origin, stale-edit rejection, protected regions, cancel and revert, incremental persistence with periodic snapshots.\
**Gate:** reverting agent work never removes newer human work.
3. **Ask and progressive layout.** Full skeleton-then-fill, contextual placement, frame expansion, cancel and retry per frame. Asks can come by voice or text, with drawings and selections as context.
4. **Annotations and threads.** Select and type, then mark and type, then mark and speak. Inferred target shown and correctable. Bindings across move, resize, and delete.\
**Gate:** ordinary drawing never starts listening or triggers the agent.
5. **Sketching and handwriting.** Raw ink first, then explicit refine actions, with the original sketch recoverable. Test Apple Pencil, finger panning, and trackpad drawing here.\
**Gate:** switching between drawing, selecting, and editing never fights modes.
6. **Interactive objects.** KaTeX equations and native editable diagrams, then Mafs graphs, then one deterministic 2D simulation. D3 for layout, Three.js when content needs 3D.\
**Gate:** either participant changes a parameter and both see the same result.
7. **Predict and compare.** Predictions, sketches, and alternatives stored as board objects. Results appear next to the originals.\
**Gate:** the board preserves how an idea changed.
8. **Voice and pointing.** Push-to-talk, mark and speak, hands-free. Phrase-level pointing by shape and part ID.\
**Gate:** interrupting stops speech and obsolete actions.
9. **Context and proactive behavior.** Debounced checks, canceled on new interaction, ignoring agent-originated changes.\
**Gate:** no self-triggering loops and no interruptions during active work.
10. **Declarative and generated visuals.** Catalog objects, then Vega-Lite and Mermaid specs, then sandboxed generated widgets with the typed bridge.
11. **Manim and `VideoShape`.** Background rendering with progress, cancellation, cached outputs, and isolated jobs.
12. **Mac shell and screen capture.** `WKWebView` wrapper, hotkey, floating window, ScreenCaptureKit, with captures feeding the annotation flow.\
**Gate:** focus, multiple displays, and permissions work without a second interaction system.
13. **Cross-device.** iPad reconnect, shared-board updates, touch controls. Trusted HTTPS for microphone access on the local network.\
**Gate:** reconnecting never loses ink, annotations, or parameter changes.

The first complete milestone is phase 8. At that point people and agents can write, draw, annotate, manipulate, speak, and point together, and the combined experience gets refined before phases 9 to 13 add more systems.

Each change is tested on the two fixed sessions, one interaction at a time, comparing the old and new versions. Tracked: wrong targets, lost or overwritten edits, response latency, unnecessary interruptions, and which version is preferred.

# tldraw agent

[Permalink: tldraw agent](https://github.com/tldraw/agent-template#tldraw-agent)

This starter kit demonstrates how to build an agent that can manipulate the [tldraw](https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw) canvas.

A chat panel on the right side of the screen lets users communicate with the agent, add context, and see chat history.
